content: The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Canadian Paediatric Society recommend that all newborns undergo bilirubin screening before being discharged from the hospital. This has become standard practice in both countries. However, the US Preventive Services Task Force has not found strong evidence to support that universal bilirubin screening reduces significant outcomes such as bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction or kernicterus. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) screening compared to visual inspection in preventing hospital readmissions for phototherapy in newborns born at 35 weeks' gestation or later. A comprehensive search was conducted in June 2023 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, ICTRP, and ISRCTN. Conference proceedings and reference lists of included studies were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized trials, cluster-randomized trials, or prospective cohort studies with a control arm that evaluated TcB screening for hyperbilirubinemia in newborns prior to hospital discharge. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were used for data collection and analysis. Treatment effects were analyzed using a fixed-effect model, with risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for categorical data, and mean differences (MD) for continuous data. The GRADE approach was applied to assess the certainty of the evidence. One RCT involving 1858 African newborns at 35 weeks' gestation or greater met the inclusion criteria. These newborns, receiving routine care in a well-baby nursery, were randomly assigned to undergo TcB screening before discharge. The study was of good methodological quality. The findings were as follows: TcB screening may reduce hospital readmissions for hyperbilirubinemia compared to visual inspection (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.46; P < 0.0001; moderate-certainty evidence). TcB screening probably has little or no effect on the rate of exchange transfusion compared to visual inspection (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.01 to 14.16; low-certainty evidence). TcB screening may increase the number of newborns requiring phototherapy before discharge compared to visual inspection (RR 2.67, 95% CI 1.56 to 4.55; moderate-certainty evidence). TcB screening probably has little or no effect on the rate of acute bilirubin encephalopathy compared to visual inspection (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 8.18; low-certainty evidence). The study did not evaluate or report on the cost of care. In conclusion, moderate-certainty evidence suggests that TcB screening may reduce hospital readmissions for hyperbilirubinemia compared to visual inspection. Low-certainty evidence indicates that TcB screening probably has little or no effect on the rate of exchange transfusion. However, moderate-certainty evidence suggests that TcB screening may increase the number of newborns requiring phototherapy before discharge. Low-certainty evidence also suggests that TcB screening probably has little or no effect on the rate of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. Since only one RCT was identified, further research is needed to determine whether TcB screening can effectively reduce readmissions and complications associated with neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. In settings where follow-up care for newborns after hospital discharge is limited, identifying those at risk for severe hyperbilirubinemia before discharge is crucial to ensure targeted follow-up care.
